title: The Cost of Prestige

reveal.headline: Affluence carries distinct physiological and behavioral trade-offs.
reveal.body: The evidence is mixed. While high-status areas offer environmental benefits like cooler temperatures, they are linked to specific behavioral risks and heightened physiological reactivity in certain groups.

explain.headline: The environment shapes your physical and social reality.
explain.body: Living in an affluent neighborhood can reduce exposure to heat-related health risks. However, these same areas are associated with a higher likelihood of intoxication, drug use, and property crime.

matters.headline: Your surroundings dictate your internal state.
matters.body: That may be why your neighborhood feels different. Your body may react to your surroundings based on your background, while your environment simultaneously alters your risk of crime or heat stress.

example.headline: The quiet of a manicured street.
example.body: You walk past a row of perfectly kept houses. The air feels cooler than the city center. You feel the weight of the status around you.

question.headline: What is your neighborhood doing to your body?

verdict: The evidence shows that affluence is associated with both specific behavioral risks and distinct physiological and environmental benefits, rather than a uniform psychological cost.
caveat: The study on physiological reactivity used simulated neighborhood environments rather than real-world living conditions.
caption: Affluence is not a uniform psychological experience. It is a complex trade-off between environmental benefits and behavioral risks. Research shows that while wealthy areas offer protection from heat, they are linked to specific social risks and unique physiological reactions. These findings are based on simulated environments and may differ in real-world living conditions. What do you notice about the atmosphere of your own neighborhood?
